slices.label: Men outside the South
slices.source: 1860 census (Eighth Census), white men 21+ outside the eleven later-Confederate states; property tests had mostly ended, and only five New England states let Black men vote on equal terms; calibrated to certified returns.

slices.label: Women outside the South
slices.source: No women could vote for president in 1860; 1860 census women 21+ shown for population only.

slices.label: White Southerners
slices.source: 1860 census, white adults in the eleven later-Confederate states; white men voted except in South Carolina, whose legislature chose its electors; the free-soil nominee was on no ballot in ten of these states; calibrated to certified returns.

slices.label: Black Southerners, most of them enslaved
slices.source: 1860 census, Black adults in the eleven later-Confederate states, overwhelmingly enslaved; enslaved people could not vote and no Southern state let free Black men vote.

slices.label: Immigrants not yet citizens
slices.source: 1860 census, foreign-born white men not yet naturalized; several Midwestern and Western states let declarant aliens vote, elsewhere only naturalized men could.

whatIfs.label: Everyone Votes
whatIfs.detail: Every adult can vote, and turns out.

runs.summary: Rerun with nothing changed, 1860 comes out as it did: Lincoln wins, 180–12–111. The closest state was Oregon, which went to Lincoln by 0.4 points. Every one of my 100 reruns reproduces it exactly.
howIGotThis: The numbers: the 1860 census counts and certified returns; every draw reproduces 1860 exactly before the change.
How sure: I reran it 100 times with different population and parameter draws.

south-white.name: Anna Reed
south-white.quote: I cannot vote myself, though my husband and I discuss the candidates. The times are troubled, and this election troubles us greatly.
south-white.controlQuote: I cannot vote myself, though my husband and I discuss the candidates. The times are troubled, and this election troubles us greatly.

men.name: Ernest Reed
men.quote: The Republican will keep the factories running and protect our wages from cheap slave labor competing in the territories. That's what matters to a working man like me.
men.controlQuote: The Republican will keep the factories running and protect our wages from cheap slave labor competing in the territories. That's what matters to a working man like me.

women.name: Ruth Robinson
women.quote: I cannot vote tomorrow—the law forbids it. My husband will cast our household's ballot.
women.controlQuote: I cannot vote tomorrow—the law forbids it. My husband will cast our household's ballot.

questions: Election Day is Tuesday. Can this person vote, how likely are they to vote, and if they vote, for whom?
A neighbour asks what this person will do on Tuesday, 6 November. Will they cast a ballot for president, and for which candidate?
Think about Tuesday's presidential election from where this person stands. How likely are they to vote, and which candidate would get their vote?
